policies.summary: Privately developed wind and solar facilities are exempt from Power Review Board approval once the owner files certifications (including local decommissioning compliance and, above 10 MW, a public meeting), leaving siting to county and city zoning; the board must still approve generation built by public power suppliers and private energy storage.

restrictions.description: Butler County has no zoning; a countywide survey (~800 responses) found roughly 90% support for a moratorium on the top land uses of concern (wind, solar, data centers, battery storage, landfill), following years of unregulated development including the in-progress Sandhills Energy solar project. Active as of 2026-09-23, though modified: adopted 2026-03-16 as a 9-month moratorium (through approximately 2026-12-15) on wind, solar, data center, battery storage, and landfill land uses while the county completes a comprehensive plan and zoning regulations (targeted for completion around September 2026). Per Flatwater Free Press, after the threat of a lawsuit the county later exempted the ongoing Sandhills Energy solar project (which had been under development since 2019) from the moratorium. Legal basis: Resolution 2026-07 (Butler County Board of Supervisors), mirroring the Planning Commission's Resolution 2026-04 but striking language that would have excluded projects already under construction.

Resident concerns raised at public comment about health, safety, and property-value impacts of proposed solar energy farms. Active as of 2026-09-23. Resolution No. 2026-08, adopted 2026-06-23 on a 6-1 vote, imposes a 6-month moratorium on accepting new conditional-use-permit applications for solar energy farms (through approximately 2026-12-23) and directs the Planning Commission to review the comprehensive plan/zoning regulations (setbacks, infrasound, health concerns, property-value impacts, 'occupied dwelling' definition, etc.) and report recommendations within 4 months. Existing operations and already-issued pending permits are not affected. Legal basis: Resolution No. 2026-08 (Fillmore County Board of Supervisors).

County zoning regulations not sufficient to address commercial wind/solar projects. Adopted 2025-08-26; a temporary moratorium on wind energy installations and solar power generation systems. No data-center-specific moratorium was located for Furnas County despite Nebraska Public Media listing the county among those with data center moratoria in place. [VERIFY details not confirmed at confidence 0.55 in the 2026-09 refresh]. Legal basis: Resolution 2025-8-26.

Regulatory-gap/preemptive: county attorney and chair described ongoing work to update the county's comprehensive plan and zoning regulations (targeted for completion by May 2027) and encouraged public participation in town-hall meetings on the update; the proposed moratorium would pause applications while that update is completed. Pending as of 2026-09-23. The Sept. 8, 2026 board agenda listed 'Consider imposing a 12 month moratorium on the acceptance of applications for wind energy systems, solar energy systems, battery energy storage systems, cryptocurrency-mining operations, data centers, artificial intelligence facilities, carbon dioxide capture, transport, and sequestration facilities, high-voltage transmission infrastructure, and other utility scale or specialized technology facilities superseding Resolution 2025-8.' At the Sept. 8 meeting the board discussed the item but did not vote (no resolution number was assigned in the minutes for this item, unlike the numbered resolutions that followed for other business). At the Sept. 21, 2026 meeting, the item returned as 'proposed Resolution 26-18'; the minutes record discussion but 'No action taken at this time.' No adoption vote had occurred as of the last confirmed meeting (Sept. 21, 2026), two days before this research date. [VERIFY adoption date not confirmed at confidence 0.6 in the 2026-09 refresh]. Legal basis: Proposed Resolution 26-18 (not yet adopted as of 2026-09-21), described in the Sept. 8, 2026 agenda as superseding 'Resolution 2025-8'.

regulatory_gap: broad pause covering utility-scale and specialized technology facilities pending county zoning/regulatory development. Active as of 2026-09-23. Resolution 2026-11, adopted 2026-06-10, imposes a 12-month moratorium on acceptance of applications for wind and solar energy systems, battery energy storage systems, cryptocurrency-mining operations, data centers, artificial intelligence facilities, carbon dioxide capture/transport/sequestration facilities, and high-voltage electric transmission infrastructure; it supersedes the county's prior 2025 moratorium resolutions (2025-19, 2025-21, 2025-25). Legal basis: Resolution 2026-11 (McPherson County Board of Commissioners), superseding Resolutions 2025-19, 2025-21, and 2025-25.

regulatory_gap: the county's zoning regulations do not yet address commercial-scale renewable energy systems; the moratorium is intended to remain in place only until new zoning regulations governing such systems are formally adopted and become legally binding. Active as of 2026-09-23. This is a distinct, longer-running moratorium from the county's separate 2026-06-30 data-center-specific moratorium already in the inventory (ne-seward-county-2026, Resolution 3937): this row covers commercial wind, solar, and battery-generated energy projects, was first imposed 2023-08-01, and has been repeatedly extended by the Board (including at its Jan. 6, 2026 meeting). Most recently, the Board voted 2026-08-25 (Resolution No. 3947, unanimous) to continue the moratorium for six more months from that date (to approximately 2027-02-25) or until new zoning regulations are adopted and legally binding, whichever comes first. It applies to solar systems of 500kW AC or greater and wind systems serving off-site customers/community/grid. Legal basis: Resolution No. 3947 (Seward County Board of Commissioners, adopted 2026-08-25), continuing the moratorium first imposed 2023-08-01 and repeatedly renewed since (cites Neb. Rev. Stat. section 23-114).

A 2018 resolution requires that wind turbines be set back 2,400 feet from neighboring dwelling units and 6,000 feet from any existing wind turbine not owned by the applicant.
As of May 2020, the Brown County Zoning Regulations require that commercial wind turbines be set back 1 mile from property lines and roads.

In March 2023, the Buffalo County Commissioners adopted new setback requirements for wind turbines that require distances of: 2 miles from any burial site or the Platte River; 3 miles from any agriculture residential zoned property; 3 miles from property lines of nonparticipants; 3 miles from any church, hospital, pool, or park; 5 miles from any village or city; 5 miles from any wildlife preservation area.

In December 2024, the Burt County Board of Supervisors adopted new zoning regulations that require commercial wind turbines to be set back 3 miles from any towns or villages, 1 mile from property lines, and 0.5 miles from any occupied dwelling.

Cedar County’s zoning ordinance, last updated in June 2022, requires commercial wind turbines to be set back at least one mile from non-participating dwelling units, public conservation lands, and other existing commercial wind turbines not owned by the applicant.

On July 26, 2021, Dakota County amended its zoning regulations to require that commercial wind turbines be set back 2 miles from neighboring dwelling units (up from 2,700 feet) and 2 miles from wetlands and other conservation lands (up from 600 feet).
In November 2022, Dawson County adopted a 1-year moratorium on wind farm applications.
In September 2015, Franklin Township implemented regulations requiring that wind turbines be set back 1,640 feet from public roads and non-participating private property lines.
Gage County adopted a moratorium on new permits for wind farms and banned commercial wind turbines within 1 mile of property lines.
In April 2024, the Greeley County Board of Commissioners adopted a 3-year moratorium on renewable energy applications.
Hamilton County ordinance requires that wind turbines be set back 2 miles from property lines of non-participating landowners.
Holt County amended its zoning ordinance in November 2022 to require commercial wind turbines to be set back at least 1 mile from neighboring dwelling units.
An ordinance last amended in January 2016 provides that solar farms of 25 kW or larger must be set back at least 1,320 feet from neighboring dwelling units.
In 2015, Lancaster County adopted updates to its zoning code to require that wind turbines maintain noise limits of 40 dBa in the day and 37 dBa at night at non-participating dwellings.

On October 28, 2020, the Wheeler County Commissioners voted to prohibit “Commercial/Utility Grade Wind Energy Systems.” On November 25, 2020, the county attorney informed the commissioners that their vote to completely prohibit utility-scale wind was unconstitutional and advised them to consider other restrictions.

Since October 2019 or earlier, Thomas County has required that wind turbines be set back 3 miles from property lines, roads, and wetlands, and limited noise to 35 dbA at the nearest occupied structure.
